text: Given the head of a singly linked list and two integers left and right, where left is at most right, reverse the nodes from position left to position right, and return the resulting list.

Let me restate it. Positions are one-indexed, and the range is inclusive on both ends. So for one, two, three, four, five with left equal to two and right equal to four, I reverse the nodes holding two, three, four and get one, four, three, two, five. Two clarifications. First — am I relinking nodes, or is swapping values acceptable?
Relink the nodes. Treat the values as opaque.
Good. Second — constraints on the input? Specifically, is right guaranteed to be within the list?
Up to five hundred nodes, and yes — one, at most left, at most right, at most n, is guaranteed. Can you do it in one pass?

I'll aim for one pass. And I want to note that guarantee explicitly, because it's what lets my reversal loop skip every null check — I'll come back to that at the end. Let me also pin the edge cases now, since this problem is mostly edge cases. Left equals right: a single node, so reversing it is a no-op. Left equals one: the head itself moves — that's the one that usually breaks people. Right equals n: the segment runs to the tail, so whatever follows it is null.

This problem reminds me of the standard three-pointer, in-place list reversal — flip one link per iteration. I already know that loop, so I'm not going to re-derive it. The new problem is the two ends. Think of the list as three chunks: prefix, segment, suffix. Reversing the middle chunk swaps its head and tail. So afterwards, the prefix must point at the new segment head, which used to be at right, and the new segment tail, which used to be at left, must point at the suffix. Two links to fix. That's the whole problem.
Do you need extra traversals to find those endpoints?

No — and that's the nice part. The reversal loop hands me all three for free. When the loop finishes, prev is sitting on the last node it flipped, the old right — the new segment head. And next is sitting on the node just past it — the suffix head. The third one I get by not moving a pointer: if I park a tail pointer on the node before the segment and never touch it, then tail's next still points at the old segment head — the new segment tail. So: one walk to position tail, one walk to reverse, then two assignments. One pass.
What about left equals one? There's no node before the segment.

Right — so I'll manufacture one. A dummy node in front of the head, and tail starts there. That collapses reverse-from-the-head and reverse-from-the-middle into the same code path, and returning dummy's next handles the head changing without a special case. I'll put it on the stack, not the heap — if I allocate it with new, nothing frees it, since I return dummy's next. That's a leak of one node per call.

Here's the plan, with one through five, left two, right four. One: walk left minus one steps from the dummy, so tail lands on node one. Two: reverse n equals right minus left plus one links in place; afterwards tail's next is node two, the new segment tail, prev is node four, the new head, and next is node five. Three: relink in this order — two's next becomes five, then tail's next becomes four. One thing I want to flag before I write it: the length is right minus left plus one, not right minus left. Inclusive range — positions two through four is three nodes.
Does the order of those two assignments matter?

Yes, and it's subtle enough that I'd want to say why out loud. The first line reads tail's next to find the new segment tail. The second line writes tail's next. Same field. So if I write first, the only pointer to node two is gone, and the other line would modify node four instead — turning four-to-three into four-to-five and dropping two nodes. It'd return one, four, five. And it would still look right when left equals right, because the segment's head and tail are the same node — so a one-node test wouldn't catch it. The fix that makes order irrelevant: stash the segment tail in a local before the reversal. If a field is both a source and a destination, copy it into a local first.

Alright, let me code this up. The middle block is exactly the standard reversal loop, with the termination swapped from until null to n times. Everything else is boundary handling: the dummy on the stack, the walk to tail, and the two relink lines in that order. The easy-to-get-wrong line is the very first one — n is right minus left plus one, because the range is inclusive.
Walk it.

One through five, left two, right four — expected one, four, three, two, five. The row that matters is the first relink: tail's next is still node two, so two's next becomes five; only then does tail's next become four. Result: one, four, three, two, five. Correct. Now the edge cases I listed. Left equals right: one loop iteration, prev and tail's next are the same node, and the relinks restore what was there. Left equals one: tail stays on the dummy, and dummy's next becomes the new head — exactly the case the dummy exists for. Right equals n: next comes out as null, which correctly terminates the list.
Your reversal loop never checks whether curr is null. Is that safe?

Only because you guaranteed right is at most n. That's borrowed safety, not inherent safety. The loop trusts the count. If right could exceed the list length, curr would walk off the end, and next equals curr's next would dereference null. Hardening it is one extra condition — loop while i is under n and curr is not null — plus a null check before the relink. I'd leave it out here: the constraint is stated, and defensive code against an impossible input just obscures the invariant. But I'd want to be able to answer this exact question, which is why I flagged the constraint up front.

Time is order right, which is linear worst case: positioning is left minus one steps, reversal is n steps — exactly right in total, and no node is visited twice. Space is constant — four pointers and a stack-allocated dummy. One alternative worth mentioning is head insertion: repeatedly lift the node after curr and splice it right behind tail. Same complexity, same single pass, and no relink step at all — so the ordering trap doesn't exist. The tradeoff is pointer writes: three per node moved versus one per node flipped, so reversing a five-hundred-node list end to end is roughly three times the writes. Last thing — this generalizes. Reversing every group of k nodes is this exact function in a loop.

Good. Three things. You separated the part you already knew from the part that was new. You didn't re-derive the reversal loop; you named it and moved on to the actual difficulty, the two endpoints. You explained the assignment order as an aliasing problem and gave the fix that makes it moot. And you identified which of my guarantees your code is leaning on, unprompted, then told me the cost of removing it. That's the difference between code that passes and code you can reason about.
